utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, to continue your cross-examination; and, General, you remain subject to the declaration you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, last week we concluded with an examination of a newspaper article published in Danas on the 20th of June, 2001. The witness was aware of its contents, the essential part of the document being an open letter of the Belgrade Lawyers' Association, and I would ask that that be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. The article in the newspaper Danas was clear from the testimony of this witness on the last occasion that he explained his role quite clearly in the Trifunovic trial. The article itself contains aspects of journalistic comment which are not regularly admitted by this Tribunal, and in my submission there is no probative additional value in addition to what this witness has already said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the article contains a succinct analysis and the expression of views by professional colleagues of this witness. He acknowledged they held and expressed those views, and this would be a convenient way to have them before you. As to the second part of the article to which we barely turned last week for want of time, I shall be dealing with it with other documents in due course in any event, so it's for the first part of the article that I want its submission -- seek its submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is to some extent difficult with the witness present, but it's not my recollection that the witness accepted that these were views that were genuinely held by personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I mischaracterise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think in the past, because of time pressures, the detail of a witness's knowledge of the content of a document being put to him is not perhaps pressed home in the way it might be if time pressures weren't as they are here. Now, if I'm wrong about that, obviously I'm quite happy to be very quickly corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add to what you said, briefly, which is this: In the transcript on the last occasion, Your Honour is absolutely correct, that this witness did not accept the allegations. He referred to them as unfounded and did not accept them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's Mr. Nice's point. Mr. Nice's point is whether he accepts that the allegations were made by these people, and if he accepts that much, then I can see something in the argument that's being presented, but it -- I mean, that's all. That's as far as it goes. It gets exhibited for that purpose. At least, that would be my own view. But my recollection isn't clear that he actually went that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask him again this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may put it to him again. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember, General Gojovic, the article from Danas that we explored under time pressures last week. I think you declined an opportunity to look at the document, saying that you didn't need to. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you accept, do you not, that the views expressed in that article were indeed the views of the lawyers who sent the open letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to their positions, there are also the comments of journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The LiveNote laptop -- there's no problem with the laptops, but if there are some technical people could take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can follow on the laptop. Continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer is that there was also some journalistic views. I'm concerned that the allegations made are the comments expressed by your colleagues, and as you've already said, you accept that those views were their views and were expressed by them.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were their views or not, I don't know. That's what they wrote, and since they acted as Defence counsel of the accused in the case that I presided over, that's it. So any further comment with respect to their positions has no foundations in facts. You received the judgement. You saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the purpose that I seek admission, the answer, it seems to me, would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I remember he said he knew of this defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. He said he didn't need to look at it because he knew of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 839.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position is this, is it not: You then wanted to become a practising lawyer. You were not allowed to become a practising lawyer. Notwithstanding that, when, for example, General Pavkovic was interviewed by the OTP, you sought to represent him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I did become a lawyer, and the bar brought up the case again, but their decision was overruled by the Supreme Court of Serbia in the legal proceedings, and they had to proceed pursuant to the law. As for Pavkovic, I attended as his legal advisor, not as his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've applied to appear at this court on behalf of one of those accused of the Vukovar crimes, and you have been declined the rights of audience here, haven't you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to represent them but they asked me to be an investigator in the Defence team, not myself as counsel. The accused addressed the Court for it to appoint me, to authorise me, to investigate as an investigator in view of the fact that I had headed the proceedings previously and I am aware of the facts. Not as Defence counsel. So don't put matters topsy-turvy, upside down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have time to deal with Sarajevo much, and if I have more time I'll return to it later, but just confirm these things, if you will: The military police in the barracks at Sarajevo where you were stationed were fully armed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had -- and had the ability to use, from those barracks, sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no sniper rifles because the police does not have snipers, sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have access to chemical materials that could have been used?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladic was regularly in contact with the barracks, was he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice by phone. I asked to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly spoke to him once yourself, but the commander of the military --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the barracks, then I asked that he receive me for me to be able to inform him of the situation, the court proceedings that were pending from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Tomcic the man in charge of the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of that military police unit. That means 120 people, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll return to that, if I have time, in due course. As to your evidence last week, and in particular as to tabs 17 and 18, your suggestion or your evidence is that here was a perfectly operating or satisfactorily operating judicial military system; is that correct? That's in summary what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you're saying, so that we can understand it and put it in its context in this trial, is such a system to be in effect is incompatible with the existence of a plan, whenever generated, to remove Kosovo Albanians by ethnic cleansing, yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. According to the federal constitution, Article 17 - take a look at it - provides for the fact that the -- a citizen of the Republic of Yugoslavia cannot be expelled from the territory of the state. They are free to move around and come back. That is a constitutional right accorded to citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be a crime to expel a citizen from Kosovo, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to international war law, this is an internal conflict. There is no expulsion here. It's an internal conflict in which the citizens left for their own safety and security. When the NATO aggression started, the citizens started to leave to safer places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, we'll come back to that. I think you misunderstood what I was trying to say by way of helpfully encapsulating the accused's case. I will say it once more so you can understand why I'm asking you the questions I'm going to ask you. If there was an effective and efficient military judicial system, then the existence of such a system is incompatible with a plan to ethnically cleanse Kosovo Albanians, because you can't be asking people to commit the crime of pushing people out of the country at the same time as having in place a system for punishing them if they commit such a crime.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you have the courts for, the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the position -- the historical position is that, as you will know, the authorities in Serbia Montenegro had received warnings right from 1998 about the possible commission of crimes on the territory of Serbia Montenegro, and in particular in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who cautioned them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you aware, for example, of letters sent by the former Prosecutor Louise Arbour to the accused in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What were the grounds for her to send those letters? Was she on the spot or did she receive intelligence reports on the part of certain armed forces?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it matter if she received intelligence reports if the warning she gave was a good warning, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But a warning must have arguments to back it up from the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're unaware of this letter, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she came out publicly, but I haven't had occasion to read the letter. She didn't send the letter to the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of the concerns expressed by General Perisic in his letter of the 23rd of July, 1998, where he referred to the -- amongst other things, to the tendency of the army to act outside the system's institutions? Are you aware of that letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army never acted outside the system's institutions. If that's what the letter says, then it's very controversial and I can't believe that Perisic said that, that the army was working outside the system. The army never acted outside the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to continue asking you questions that are susceptible to a yes or no answer but you must take your own course as how you reply to them. Are you aware of a letter from Louise Arbour, the former Prosecutor, of the 15th of October, 1998 to the accused indicating an intention to resume her investigations into Kosovo, desiring to visit the place?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it except through the press. There were certain articles with headings to that effect, but I don't know the contents. Just a moment. Why didn't she approach the prosecutor, for example? Why would she approach the president? She's a prosecutor, so she should approach her colleague the prosecutor on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have your answer. Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a letter sent by the British Prime Minister Tony Blair on the 24th of September 1998 to the accused, expressing concern about the developing humanitarian crisis and so on? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I wasn't a member of the government for Prime Ministers to send me letters. I was president of the military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are all exhibits. I can give you the numbers if you want them, but I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that after Racak several publications asserted that there had been a massacre there? For example, the OSCE made an almost immediate report alleging that the VJ and police had attacked Racak.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I followed that in the press, but army did not attack Racak, so the OSCE report is incorrect in that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- remind us: Your source of knowledge that the army didn't attack Racak is one -- one informant, isn't it? You never conducted any investigation, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't conduct an investigation because it didn't come under our purview. The army didn't take part in it, so we didn't investigate. It was the court in Pristina that conducted the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to hear about that from the next witness, but your pride in the army, your concern that the army should have a proper judicial legal system leads me to ask this: If there was, as there was, public international allegations that the army was involved in Racak, did not the military judiciary owe a duty to investigate? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegations have to be backed up by proof and evidence. Just to claim something publicly internationally doesn't mean a thing. There was a group of armed terrorists and this was a mission without any arms. So where do you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may look at the legal position of the obligations of the legal -- of the military judicial system later, but just so that I can have your answer clearly, it wouldn't matter to you, would it, General Gojovic, how many newspapers, how many television programmes suggested that the army was involved, you wouldn't investigate on the basis of such material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up to the prosecutor. I wasn't the prosecutor at that time. So it's up to the prosecutor. And since the prosecutor didn't react, it means he analysed it and found there were no elements to do so. He investigated the facts through the military command and didn't find --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General, can you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I didn't say that he checked them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you did.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I said I wasn't the prosecutor at that time but the prosecutor probably checked it out. If I were the prosecutor, I would have done so, but as I say, I wasn't the prosecutor so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somewhere in the archives of the VJ, there should be a report, or in the archives of the military judiciary to which you would have access in your term of office, there should be a report, should there, from the current or the then judge charged with investigating, there should be a report showing that the VJ were not involved. Have you seen such a report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen a report like that, and I don't believe it exists in the military judiciary organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of February of 1999, General Drewienkiewicz wrote to the accused in this case, dealing with allegations of looting in particular on a widespread basis, again alleging the matter against the VJ and the MUP. Were you aware of that letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that letter, but the investigating organs would have taken steps for any looting when it came to members of the Yugoslav army in 1999, but you're mentioning a date that doesn't fall within that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 26th of March of 1999, Louise Arbour wrote again, saying that it was her intention to investigate all serious violations of international humanitarian law. Were you aware of that letter being sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She issued such warnings on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look, if we may, at a short clip which is already exhibited, Exhibit 15. Thank you very much. This is not absolutely date specific but perhaps you'd be good enough to watch it with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not getting any sound. There should be sound on this. Without the sound, it's of no practical use because it's the soundtrack I want. Thank you very much. We'll cancel that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, as I'm going to suggest, there were broadcasts on the BBC and CNN alleging that ethnic cleansing was happening and that the VJ were involved - and Exhibit 15 is one such example, Your Honours, when we get the soundtrack back - was that something that was brought to the attention of the military judicial system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the images here, but when we speak about ethnic cleansing, this example cannot be applied to Kosovo and Metohija where we're dealing with citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and, pursuant to the constitution, they cannot be expelled from the country. So these were people who were endeavouring to save themselves from the NATO aggression and the terrorist forces in conflict with the army of Yugoslavia and other armed forces --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, General, that if there was an allegation that the military were responsible for evacuating people from their homes, that the military judicial system would not investigate it as long as they remained within Serbia, on technical grounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? When somebody says "responsible," then you need to back it up with arguments. You can't on the basis of theoretic fiction make conclusions of reality and paint a picture of reality. And now, on assumption, you want to see how the public prosecutor reacted, or military prosecutor. You must work on facts, not the fictitious writings of newspaper agencies or newspapers or people roaming around and reporting from a distance. You must assess the realistic state of affairs, and the judiciary deals with realistic facts, realistic changes in the world, realistic cause and effect, not fiction, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not fictitious and theses and assumptions. The prosecutor analysed the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, it doesn't help for you to deliberately misunderstand the question. You understood the question I asked you perfectly well, and you've given an answer which bears no relationship to the question at all, but I'm not going to take up time. Move on, please, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the prosecutor must react if there is something that has been contrary -- done contrary to the law, but he had no proof in that direction to lead him to that conclusion. So we do understand each other very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, I asked you a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather we've got the soundtrack. Just remind ourselves of Exhibit 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It shouldn't have a soundtrack. I remember making the objection. This is the videotapes produced by the Investigator Spargo and it was to be without soundtrack because there are over three and a half hours of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for different reasons but the soundtrack is now what's important because it makes allegations against the VJ. I really don't desire to take time -- may I play it with the soundtrack and we'll see if it can be exhibited with the soundtrack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only very short, about a minute, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Village by village, hour after hour, under the symbols of their nationalism, the Serbian authorities pushed the Albanian population of Kosovo into exile. By now the refugees have been stripped of any document that says who they are. Only their despair is left as a mark of common identity. This is not haphazard flow of people. There is a grim logic to what is going on. When you check where these refugees are coming from, you can see that Kosovo is being cleansed, ethnically cleansed, village by village hour after hour. "The authorities here do their best to monitor where the refugees come from. Their list reveals an expulsion of industrial efficiency. "Can you show me on the map? "Starting with the outlying regions of Kosovo, Serb forces have moved remorselessly towards the interior, pushing towards the capital, Pristina. And as if to prove --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we don't get more detail than a reference to the authorities pushing people out and pushing them to another country. The authorities could be either the police or the military. If you'd seen that terribly serious allegation, would you have thought it right, as the chief military prosecutor, to investigate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not chief military prosecutor. It was another colleague. He looked at these matters, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was put on the basis of a hypothesis. Had you seen it, would you have investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have investigated, and I would have established whether what the reporter is saying is correct or not, but obviously it was impossible. It was impossible. Legally or in real terms. But if we want to look at things hypothetically, then my answer is yes, I would have investigated it because nobody is allowed to expel anyone, according to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a very small clarification. The interpreter said, "Would you, as chief military prosecutor..." which in Serbian means only whether that was the case in real terms, whether he was actually the chief military prosecutor. It's ambiguous in Serbian. So when you say "If you were the chief military prosecutor," it's ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the question was, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, when I put the question to him, I omitted that reference, and he gave the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of your last answer, there -- one preliminary question: You are aware, not only -- not only by the Prosecution in this court but in all sorts of other publications - Human Rights Watch, OSCE - the allegation has been fairly and squarely made that thousands were killed and tens and tens of thousands expelled from Kosovo as a planned ethnic cleansing involving the MUP and the VJ. You're aware of that, aren't you? Those allegations have been made.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put such leading questions, as if I knew that there was ethnic cleansing, and precisely what I've been saying to you was that there was no ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... trying to get you to listen to the questions. You're a general. That requires a Ph.D., I think, to qualify in the former Yugoslavia. You must be able to understand -- you didn't have a Ph.D., but that's the level of academic attainment required. You must be able to follow the question. Are you aware - yes or no - that such allegations have been made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do have a master's degree in law, in criminal law, so please don't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just listen to the question. The question is whether you're aware, whether you know that allegations have been made of ethnic cleansing by the MUP and the VJ, just whether you are aware of the allegations that have been made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such allegations were made. Such allegations were made by different --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of them were made while you were in charge, the allegations, weren't they? Radio, television, Human Rights Watch, and so on, many of those allegations were made while you were in charge.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "in charge"? What do you mean that I was in charge?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can only borrow the words of the accused who summarised, if I can find it rapidly, your position as being in charge, I think, of the legal -- military legal service, when you were made presiding judge. Were you not the man in charge at one stage? Yes, here we are: "I was appointed to the position of head of the legal department of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia." And I think that was then picked up on one or two occasions by the accused in questions. Were you not the head of the legal department of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was, and that is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of the allegations of ethnic cleansing were made while you were the man in charge. And you know what the next question is, so I'll ask it: Where is the inquiry that you conducted or organised to be conducted into ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no evidence of ethnic cleansing, and there were no criminal proceedings instituted against a single individual on such grounds. The military courts have all their records available, and then the prosecutor has to deal with charges, not the legal department of the army. The legal department of the army set up the system, organised it, the system of the military judiciary. And it did function. So if ethnic cleansing occurs as a crime, then the prosecutor in charge has to press charges. However, since this did not happen, the prosecutor did not indict anyone and, therefore, it never happened. And I already mentioned what the reasons were, why there could not have been any ethnic cleansing. The Serb population accounts for a very small percentage of the population of Kosovo, 10 or 15 per cent. Who is going to populate such vast areas if a majority of the population is expelled, the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The simple answer to my question is this, isn't it, there were widespread allegations from many sources of ethnic cleansing and you did nothing whatsoever to investigate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, he -- he said that it would be the prosecutor who would be press charges, the legal department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check whether the prosecutor made an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neither you as the man in charge nor any prosecutor made an investigation. And I'm grateful to His Honour for requiring me to reformulate the question. Neither you as the man in charge nor any prosecutor made an investigation into ethnic cleansing, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor looked at the matter. I talked to the chief military prosecutor. I did talk to him. He looked into it, and his findings were that there were no elements for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you discuss this with him and where is the written report of such an important decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a discussion when there were such things appearing in the world media, and we had this professional discussion, but legally it was not possible for this to happen in our country, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've made references today and you made references on the last occasion to the impossibility of investigating matters such as this. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a constitutional principle. It is a right guaranteed to the citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by the constitution. No one can expel a citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it cannot be qualified as --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- it's my mistake for not having made my question simple enough, so I'll make it more simple. Last time and this you said it was impossible to investigate certain matters in Kosovo. Why was it impossible?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I said that it was impossible, because of the safety of the agencies that were supposed to carry this out. You are losing sight of the fact that 19 countries of the strongest military alliance in the world attacked that area, that small area. You have to take the facts and figures from NATO. Let them give you their figures, how many sorties there were; 800 per day, at least, up to 1.200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's pause there, shall we? The duty to investigate on one body or another serious crime does not end with the ending of the conflict, does it? The duty to investigate continues.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but we do not have legal jurisdiction in Kosovo now. Again, you're losing sight of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying -- because that's what I wanted you to turn your attention to for us. Are you saying that it would have been impossible for your authorities to investigate matters in Kosovo if you'd really wanted to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of anything done in contravention of the law, an investigation would have been carried out. Now, we're not going to look at assumptions. If somebody assumes something, we are not going to investigate that. However, whatever happened in real terms would have been investigated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I asked you if it was impossible for your authorities or for the authorities to investigate matters in Kosovo if you really wanted to. Can you answer that question? Was it impossible or was it possible to go to Kosovo and investigate matters?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a relative possibility. You are seeking only things in an absolute sense. There is no absolute. I have already told you what all the hindrances were in terms of investigating everything that was a crime from a legal point of view. You want to say that there was a crime of ethnic cleansing that occurred in legal terms, and that is where our views differ. We cannot have matching questions and answers because we are proceeding from different premises. You are representing an indictment for which you do not have the proper argumentation. You have a fact which is movement of the population, and that is not challenged. Camps were prepared there in advance. The Red Cross were there. And wherever there is a conflict, an armed conflict, there are refugees. So this was an armed conflict, and it was expected --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept - yes or no - that if you wanted to go to Kosovo or if other authorities wanted to go to Kosovo to question witnesses, to question victims and to find out if ethnic cleansing had happened, it would be impossible to do so?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period? Which period are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2001, 2002, 2003. A period after these --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that the next witness from whom we are expecting to hear, Slavisa Dobricanin, was able certainly to conduct investigations on the territory of Kosovo in 2001, 2003?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobricanin is a forensic expert. He is an expert. He's not a law enforcement agency. The authorities conducting these proceedings called him in as an expert and not a single --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, when the witness answered "We were not allowed to go" in response to the question "Which period are you referring to?" "2001, 2002, 2003."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that needs to be followed up because it's relevant to the question of the duty to continue with the investigations after the conflict, and if there is an explanation for that, we need to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why you say there would have been no possibility for you to go, whereas Dobricanin -- I'm sorry, he's not the next witness, he's the next witness but one or two, but he could go and conduct inquiries in those years?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I've explained this but obviously you don't want to listen to me or you don't want to understand what I'm saying. Dobricanin is a forensic expert, and he carries out post-mortems as an expert at the request of the authorities, UNMIK, in charge of the investigations, whereas our investigation agencies do not have access to Kosovo and Metohija. That is on the basis of the Military Technical Agreement that was signed. Not a single authority can act there. He goes as an expert upon their request. He does not conduct inquiries. He gives his expert opinion in terms of the identification of corpses, the wounds that were sustained, et cetera. I think that that should be quite clear to the Prosecutor and to all the parties in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, throughout the world day and daily police forces carry out investigations in other countries over which they have no jurisdiction by asking the authorities in these other countries to investigate matters for them or to cooperate with them in the investigation. Why would it not be possible in Serbia, after the conflict, for cooperation to take place in the investigation of allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. Cooperation was asked for, but on the other side the representatives of UNMIK did not accept that. That's the problem. They do not accept that, or they simply remain silent. But they do not refuse such requests either. The prosecutors addressed them several times, but they never got any response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in answer to -- or in development to the answer to His Honour's question, are you saying - and if so, I shall seek from you chapter, verse, and document - are you saying that there were any requests from the authorities of Serbia and Montenegro to go to the territory of Kosovo in order to investigate the widespread international allegations of ethnic cleansing that had been made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I was speaking about what the judiciary authorities did, not the agencies of the government of Serbia and Montenegro. The military prosecutors and the military organs addressed the relevant agencies of UNMIK in Kosovo and Metohija, and they did not get any return information from them concerning the possibility of investigating crimes, because they are in charge of carrying out such proceedings. There is the UNMIK organs that are in charge of this. They have their own judiciary, they have their own investigations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stop --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask them for a report and then you'll get an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you. I'm going to repeat the question because it had a detail in it that I suggest you did understand: Were there requests from your body, from any other authorities to your knowledge, to go to Kosovo to investigate ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests. Information was sought about certain events, and they also asked for certain witnesses, but there were no answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try once more, but I'm not sure you've answered my question. Were there requests -- was there any request, even one, to investigate allegations of ethnic cleansing? If yes, I'm going to want to know when, where, where the document is, and so on. So I'll repeat the question: Was there any requests, even one, to investigate allegations of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are moving the question to the area of ethnic cleansing, but I've already answered that question. I've given you a comprehensive answer. If you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. Mr. Nice, the general referred earlier to a Military Technical Agreement that prevented anybody from going there. Those were his words. I would like to find out from the general what agreement is this, between what entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Military Technical Agreement was the agreement between the representatives of the army of Yugoslavia and the representatives of the NATO forces. It was signed in Kumanovo and on the basis of this agreement all armed forces withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija and all government authorities, and authority was temporarily taken over by the United Nations and they were exercising authority, government, over the area of Kosovo and Metohija. The judiciary is a very important branch of government in any state. So not a single state agency can appear there, only humanitarian organisations. That is the central issue in this regard. As for ethnic cleansing, I've already given an answer. There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, and I'm now going to come, as I forecast right at the beginning, to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm disappointed that you are, Mr. Nice. I thought we might have got an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'll try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try once more with a very simple question that I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try once more with a very simple question that I had posed, General, first of all, and I'm going to try and repeat it. Was there a request, even one, to investigate allegations of ethnic cleansing made to the UNMIK authorities? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, whether there were any requests to that effect. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if I was refocusing on the question Your Honour had in mind, but the answer that's been given by the witness right now is that he was not aware of any such requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, General, when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, he's giving a legal answer to your question, saying that there was an agreement, an UNMIK agreement. We don't know what it says. UNMIK has jurisdiction. I don't know whether that -- by that agreement Serbia was prevented from carrying out the investigations. This is what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me develop it just another question so to make my position clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the question that His Honour Judge Bonomy asked about police forces operating under requests on the territory of other states, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it, but I am not aware of any possibility of the authorities of a foreign country conducting an investigation in another country. It can only be done through INTERPOL, but I do not know of a single case when one country can send investigators to another country to investigate a matter. I'm not aware of any such thing. If this does exist somewhere, I'm truly sorry for my lack of knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are extremely acquainted with the whole business of requests for assistance given in terms of legal proceedings because you for a long time were on the committee that represented the VJ in asserted cooperation with the ICTY, and that committee received and processed many requests for assistance. So you know how requests for assistance work, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for assistance, yes, yes. But carrying out a direct investigation by the agencies of one state on the territory of another state, that is something that I've never heard of. I'm not aware of such practice. However, assistance, yes, that's fine, and that is also envisaged in the Law on Criminal Procedure on the basis of a previously reached agreement between two states, and the principle of reciprocity applies in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, was there anything in the Military Technical Agreement to which you've referred concluded at the end of the conflict that would have prevented the authorities in Serbia making a request to UNMIK to carry out an investigation into ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no such explicit provision as far as I can remember. It is a very voluminous document, including several annexes. However, several requests were submitted for legal assistance in the case of several crimes, but there was no answer. But that military investigation agencies can conduct an investigation in Kosovo, no. In that agreement, it is stated explicitly that the military and the police are withdrawing completely, including all their equipment. What was envisaged was that up to 1.000 persons may return, but this has not been allowed until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Military Technical Agreement is paragraph 108 of the Kosovo indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we look at the material --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask: General, under that agreement -- General, under that agreement, who would have the power to investigate the crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the territory of Kosovo specifically? The new UNMIK organs that were established. However, the organs of Serbia Montenegro can act in their own territory but they have no access to Kosovo, and all possible evidence is there. Witnesses, events, et cetera. So in order to be able to investigate whether some action was a crime, whether it was illegal, you have to go to the site itself. Otherwise, one cannot get a full picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documents you've produced, we may have time to go through the business of production of documents a bit more fully, but the documents you've produced are all that there is, really, in summary form to reveal investigations that were conducted - and I have in mind tabs 17 and 18 - correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were appointed to this job by Ojdanic, who is actually a good friend of yours, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not appointed to Ojdanic. Ojdanic was duty-bound by the law to propose it to the president of the republic, and Ojdanic got the proposal from the president of the supreme military court and military prosecutor. They tabled the proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic is not a friend. He's an officer whom I respect and hold in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the long lead-up of complaints and inquires that we looked at earlier this morning into events in Kosovo, it would have been quite impossible to run this conflict or to take part in this conflict without some form of judicial military body in place; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't follow your question. How can the judicial body organise something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it another way: The eyes of the world had already on focused sharply on possible crimes and the need to investigate crimes, and in those circumstances, when this conflict started, it would have been quite impossible for the VJ not to have some form of military judicial position in place if it was to be able to give the semblance of complying with international norms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this question is highly improper, especially after long testimony providing such a great number of documents on the work of courts, of people accused and convicted during the bombing. I really don't understand that it is possible to ask a question like this that somebody wants to have system that must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- act as representing the law and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite obviously the Prosecutor does not wish to understand some things here intentionally, not that he cannot. I said that it is a legal obligation. With the proclamation of a state of war, the imperative norm is to set up judiciary organs during a state of war. So there's no dilemma there. As soon as the government decided to proclaim a state of war, automatically on the basis of the law judiciary organs are developed which act in wartime, and the day that a state of war ceases to exist, then those military judiciaries cease to exist. So it's not somebody's will, whether they want to act in one way or another because the world public opinion says so. It's a provision in the law. I think we're all men of the law, and when you have laws in a country, they come into force as provided for, and this is not brought into any political context of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest that the system over which you presided to the extent that you did was providing, so far as serious crimes are concerned, window dressing at the best. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. And the military judiciary is now being abused by what you said. Look at the gravity of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 43 in the B/C/S version of tab 17.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that tab. You didn't give it back to me. I handed it over. Could I please have it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the English page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it properly on this copy. I would like to have the document that I gave over for photocopying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 56 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're giving me is tab 18 now. I need tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 17, page 56 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 43 in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, 43 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're finding a copy of that to make available to you, don't -- have you found it now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is the case originally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the case originally involving Slobodan Stosic and one, two, three, four, five, six others. Before I come to the questions I'm going to ask you about this, it's as well that we should remember or remind the Judges that it fits in a document which is almost exclusively concerned with trivial crime, doesn't it? Comparatively trivial crime; thefts, presumably looting of one kind or another, yes? I can flip through and see but locked in the middle is this allegation against Slobodan Stosic. Now, you said, when answering questions about this, the following, at page 67: "This was uncovered in mid-April and a report was sent to the prosecutor, and the prosecutor undertook proceedings." Can you think back, please, General Gojovic, and tell us who it was that required this investigation to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor is the sole authorised individual to require an investigation to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe, but now just turn your mind back. Who in whatever way actually initiated this prosecution so that it had to be prosecuted? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody must have informed the prosecutor. Somebody had to inform him, whether somebody from the unit, a unit commander or somebody else, it doesn't say here in the review that I have. But the prosecutor tabled the request which means that he received information. Now, who he received information from is not the essential point here. What is important is the prosecutor learned about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, in the papers that have been made available to us, and we've tried to get from the authorities all the papers about prosecutions, it isn't revealed who made the original complaint, but we actually know from evidence in the case. You see, it was Aleksandar Vasiljevic who has told us the following: That he was aware - it was specific knowledge that he had got - that volunteers named Dugi and Oto, and we can see Oto as Palinkos, Dugi may be the man unnamed at the bottom, but in any event, Vasiljevic went on -- General Vasiljevic went on to say that he got the knowledge that these volunteers liquidated six or seven Albanian civilians and threw them into a well in the village of Gornja Klina. Then they dug the well up. And he went on to explain that he found out about the case and he ordered a military police patrol to be sent there to carry out the on-site investigation. Now, then, you know who Aleksandar Vasiljevic is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back, can you now remember that this particular and -- this particular investigation into a very serious crime was actually carried out because somebody senior, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, demanded that it be carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't know about that portion of Vasiljevic's statement, but the court acts upon the prosecutor alone, and you said he told the organs of the military police. The organs of the military police are organs of detection and to the organs of detection, the organs of the military police and military security are led by the head of the security department, and Vasiljevic was the number two man. He was the deputy head of the department. So that would come under his purview, to uncover the perpetrators of crimes. And when he learnt about it and he had to receive information down there at the base, not in Belgrade. He got the information from the base, and then that came under his competence and authority, precisely that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is -- this is your memory now or is this a hypothetical answer?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not memory, but it is the provision of the law that says -- spells it out. You can't work outside the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vasiljevic was relieved of his position not so very long after this. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. After me. I retired before him. I had completed my years of service and retired before him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to remind the Judges of this particular investigation, Stosic, the lieutenant colonel, was the subject of a discontinuance, and it was only the minor players, the junior ranks, the privates and the reserves, who were dealt with. Stosic lives free at the moment, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's look at the only other really serious matters. There's another one in tab 17, but we haven't got time to go into that now. We'll go to tab 18, if we may. Just to remind the Judges and get the picture back in our minds. On page 4 of the English, which is I think page 4 in the B/C/S -- no, it's page 2 in the B/C/S. Page 2 in the B/C/S. We see there on your tab 18 now it's only the junior ranks that are now all forwarding for prosecution. Apparently, so you told us, acting without any authority from the man who had taken them there, the senior officer. General Gojovic, was this the truth, that allegations of serious crimes would only ever be investigated when for one reason or another you had no choice but to investigate them and the rest of your time was focused on the trivial matters of theft of a hair-dryer and theft of a cassette and theft of a motor car?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a review here of the legal proceedings taken against individuals not for peripheral or minor offences, although you do include minor offences in your indictment as well - looting, theft of property and so on - so you have a review of all the cases where the perpetrators were identified and legal proceedings were taken against them. Where they were not identified but where the crimes were identified, and you saw from the review how many of those cases there were, over 600 - 601, I believe - so for 601 victims which you have in your indictment as well and for which you investigated for a full five or six years was investigated in the space of two months. So those comparisons of yours don't hold water. And here we're dealing with direct perpetrators, the ones that were uncovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's -- I'm only going to be able in the time available to be able to deal with a few inquiries or crimes by way of example, but just to refamiliarise the Chamber with tab 18 before I come to my next point, can we go in the English to page 6 and in the B/C/S to page 4. Now, we see here some serious, very serious crimes. Just look at the first one, numbers 1 and 2, which we looked at on the last occasion. This is where in Susica village Petrovic and Stamenkovic -- I beg your pardon, Petrovic ordered Stamenkovic and Jovic to liquidate two, an elderly man and woman, because they hadn't left the village. Well, now, you can turn my -- can you take me to a piece of paper that's going to show how this particular investigation was triggered?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the list of cases, trials. I didn't have a list like that before me. This is a brief information report from the court in Nis, and all three were convicted. You had a note, I believe, on your photocopy that somebody wrote in later on, and that note is indeed correct. This -- number 1 was first of all accused of the crime and convicted and got nine years, and the other man got seven, and I think that the judgement came into force. They were convicted, but the prosecutor re-termed the crime war crime against the civilian population. So four other people were convicted, two officers as you say, and you were given those notes and reports from the court. But I see that you're not commenting on that, whereas you were provided with a list of those crimes where two officers were convicted. One got a seven-year sentence and the other five years, and the other perpetrators got four years' imprisonment and three years' imprisonment, so you do have those facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, all I want is your assistance, if you can give it to me, on what it was that triggered --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- this investigation in the first place, and then I'll make my suggestion to you again and we'll look at another example. Can you point me to what it was that triggered this investigation? Who found it? Who decided there had to be an investigation, and so on? Can you point me to --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should look at the list of cases and find it there. I'm sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. General, listen to the question. Either you can answer it or you can't. Can you say how this particular investigation started? Who triggered it? How did it start? Either you know or you don't know. We don't need to have a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you. No, I'm not going to hold a speech, but you're quite obviously not listening to what I'm saying. All I know is set down here in this document. And let me repeat: The investigation is conducted on the -- by the court pursuant to a request from the prosecutor, and now you are mixing up who uncovered the crime and who investigated it, because it's only on the basis of the -- of a request made by the prosecutor that the court takes steps. Now, who reported the crime, I don't know. All I know is that the prosecutor learned about it and set the works in motion. And according to our laws, a criminal proceedings is put into place when the prosecutor tables a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, General, the summary makes this look to be a classical example of killing in the course of ethnic cleansing, and it's been summarised in that way. Two people, they wouldn't leave the village, so they were shot and killed. Now, I don't know if you know this, but that's similar to a number of allegations made in this case. So it's going to help us if we can find out what it was that actually triggered this investigation in the way that we happen to know from Aleksandar Vasiljevic's evidence what it was that triggered the earlier investigation, and that's why I want your help. Can you take us to the original documents, to the source of why this investigation, this particular investigation, started?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this here, we can see that unless -- if they didn't leave the village, they were killed, and that's why the whole case was taken court. So that is an argument contrary to what you are insisting. I don't know the details. I would have to look at the lists of the cases. I really can't give you the details. And the documents. But they were convicted for having behaved in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move to my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do, I think you said, General, that there were more people convicted than are shown in this summary we have. Are the details of the other convictions somewhere in tab 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There are three men concerned here, three persons, with respect to the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they were the only ones that you were speaking of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the previous ones we discussed. But I mentioned in passing that there were four others that the prosecutor knows about but isn't presenting here, four others, because he got the files and the lists, but they are not contained in this tab, because the people were convicted later on, after this tab and document was compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things you said was that that part of the investigation was labelled as a war crime; is that right? Have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are we talking about now? What do you mean? Which war crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had thought --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This event. This event here, these three men we're talking about now, they were first accused of killing several persons, but then the indictment was changed, and they were -- answered to war crimes, which is in fact a lesser -- of lesser severity than the first charge of killing, murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It appears here under Article 47, which is multiple murder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how the trial started, the proceedings started, but it ended in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to these three accused it ended as a conviction for war crimes; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the B/C/S there was the handwritten amendment, the witness not knowing in whose hand it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gojovic -- Mr. Gojovic, in your earlier answer, you said you could not give the details unless you took a look at the list of cases. Could you explain what the document is being referred to, "list of cases"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, the files of the cases. Not list of cases but the files, the criminal files containing all the proof and evidence on which the judgement was made. So I meant files of the cases. Not lists but files for the criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, although I shan't have time to go through them, the remaining cases referred to of multiple murders might also appear to fit with cases that were instituted in respect of ethnic cleansing but we don't know how they were triggered because we don't have the source papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must -- may I confirm something before I forget it, General Gojovic, and I may not have time to go through the whole process of seeking documents, although I shall try to deal with some of it. You said last week that tab 18 was provided in January -- in January 2004, and my recollection was different, but I've been able to check the matter and indeed this document was provided, probably by correspondence in the end or autumn of 2003, coming to us in the beginning of 2004, but it wasn't connected to this witness's evidence until he gave evidence last week. Can I now turn to someone else for your comments. Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic. He was one of your judges, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he wasn't a judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Deputy prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Experienced man.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] didn't have experience in prosecutors' affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know for the purposes of the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, the answer was -- reads as "I didn't have experience in prosecutors' affairs," as if the witness was speaking about himself, whereas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the answer was "he."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained how for the purposes of the Kosovo conflict reservists were called into action. You spoke of 125 altogether, including people who had been working in employment exchanges or matters of that sort, but Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic was not such a reservist, was he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to put you right there, and I do apologise. I'd like to ask the Presiding Judge to enable me to do so. No judge came from an employment exchange. They were all prosecutors and judges from district and municipal courts, with a great deal of experience working in the field, not from employment exchanges of any kind. I don't know what kind of manipulation that is. They were judges who were appointed, and they had a great deal of experience in the municipal courts and district courts. So please don't put questions like that here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading from the transcript, General Gojovic, but --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the interpretation I received. I don't know English. That's what I was said, that they were brought in from the employment exchanges --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on from that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which is not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the person you mentioned, he was an officer. He was a legal man. He worked in the prosecutor's office for a short space of time and was replaced because he couldn't do his job properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And don't refer to him, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to be put in a position which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because he tells the truth about what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened was this, wasn't it: That he went down to Kosovo and he showed enthusiasm to charge people against whom evidence existed, and that led to his eventually being sent back so that he shouldn't perform his function. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. He had full authority to raise indictments. But what he wanted to do was to kill his deputy because they got drunk and did silly things. And that's why he was replaced. So that's why I said don't put me in a difficult position here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a physical conflict between him and either his deputy or his superior, but before that, he had been bringing complaints and seeking to lay indictments --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had been seeking to bring indictments and had been thwarted from doing so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. He had full authority to bring indictments. Nobody could prevent him from doing so, nor did anybody prevent him from doing so. Nobody like that existed who would prevent him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he laid a complaint against you -- or he laid a complaint against judges and other people of the army's military court and military district command, he laid a complaint on the 13th of June, 2001, making allegations as to how he had been effectively thwarted in his work, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. He wasn't thwarted in his work, and the time that he brought in the complaint is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, did -- the question you were asked was did he make a complaint against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Complaint against me? I don't know about that, that he laid a complaint against me to anyone. And he had no reason to do so either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make a complaint against, as I suggested, unidentified judges of the military court and military district command in Pristina and members of the army and security organs and military police at the said command? Did he make such a complaint?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he did or not, because that would come under the competence of the prosecutor. He could send it to the supreme prosecutor. But whether he did or didn't, I don't know. I was not informed of any such thing, and I was the head of the legal department in the ministry of department -- in the ministry. I was not in the General Staff any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And criminal charges were raised against them because of the conflict. So maybe it was in that case, in those proceedings against him that the prosecutor raised a complaint. And that had nothing to do with the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd hoped to have finished in one session and that would have kept me to 50 per cent of the examination-in-chief. Not entirely as a result my own fault, I hope, things have gone rather more slowly but there is -- I shall simply have to make a selection of what's outstanding, but there's a lot of important stuff. I'll try to deal with it in half an hour, but I can't promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We won't quarrel if you take 55 per cent. We'll take a break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, before we return to the history of your dealings with Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic, which I'm going to deal with now sequentially or chronologically, a couple of matters of correction or detail from the answers you've already given. First, as to UNMIK, its legal authority was only in respect of the territory of Kosovo and it would never have had jurisdiction to investigate crimes of ethnic cleansing committed by Serb soldiers resident in Serbia, would it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, the suggestion that UNMIK would be non-cooperative with a legitimate request by Serbia made in any formal way to give assistance for the investigation of crimes by seeing witnesses is, I suggest, a ridiculous suggestion. UNMIK inevitably would have wanted to cooperate had you made or had anybody made such a request to them.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already given you an answer, that the prosecutors found that there no grounds for issuing an indictment for ethnic cleansing because there had been none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next point, and I've got the documents but I don't want to display them or take time displaying them unless it's essential -- or not displaying them, showing them. Do you accept that as of 2001, a court in Nis trying a rape allegation in respect of an alleged rape committed in Kosovo during the conflict would have been able to secure the attendance from Kosovo of a Kosovo witness, namely the alleged victim of the rape case? Do you accept that that level of cooperation was possible?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which court are you speaking about, a military court or a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
