utterances.text: An allegation that certainly started in a military court. It may have transferred to a civil court, but one way or another, do you accept that there would be no difficulty in securing the attendance of witnesses from Kosovo in Nis in the year 2001?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the military court is concerned, I have information that a request was sent to UNMIK and there was no response on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In which case, then, I'm going to hand you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely -- precisely as far as rape is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to hand you a document, not for display because of the protection of rape victim witnesses, and just look at this statement, please, and tell me if you're asserting that this is one of the names where a request for assistance to UNMIK was made and rejected. And then I'll make copies available for the Judges, if necessary, but it may be you'll accept from me on this occasion. The papers you're looking at now the same or a different case from those where you say cooperation was refused?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to identify the persons involved here with the information regarding the two cases I mentioned, but the names do not seem to match.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I suggest --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, though. Possibly. I mean, I do not preclude the possibility altogether, but I don't see the names match from this statement and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take the names of the accused which are here and just show that to the witness. I really don't want to add to the burden of files with documents if it's avoidable. Is that the same or different from the case you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Then that's it, yes. If it has to do with this indictment, yes. Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you accept, and we needn't burden the Court with the papers, you accept that on the occasion that I've shown you, which was in 2001, there could be cooperation in the provision of witnesses from Kosovo to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it existed in fact, but I know that requests were sent and that there was no response for a while. As for later, I did not check.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can have those papers back. They're available to the Court, the accused, and the assigned counsel, if wanted, but I don't want to, as I said, burden us with detail if it's avoidable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next thing before we move on, is it right that so far as serious crimes, chargeable as war crimes or otherwise, serious crimes arising from the conflict, there were convictions only in respect of Ivan Nikolic, Dragisa Petrovic, and Mancic, those three cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it looks on the basis of the information that I have here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... person convicted was a captain?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class, and a major. Mancic is a major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No colonels, generals or anybody else investigated, let alone charged?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no evidence to the effect that they had perpetrated anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the ones that we've looked at and for the reasons that I've already explored, we can't say what it was that triggered those particular investigations that led to convictions, can we, because we haven't got the documents here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was their illegal action that led to this, and are you seeking a more specific answer? One has to look at the case file in order to be able to give that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've produced a lot of material, tabs 1 to 16, going to show that there was in place instructions for and statutes for and rules for compliance with the rules of war and for the operation of a proper military judicial system. Are you acquainted with the evidence of the witness here, Peter -- or General Sir Peter de la Billiere who expressed concern -- or not concern, surprise at the fact that there should be so much material? Are you acquainted with that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was saying he was surprised at the volume of orders or the need for them to be reiterated at such regular intervals.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which orders was he referring to? I only referred to two orders here and one aide-memoire, which is not an order. Only two orders from the Supreme Command level, which is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was his evidence. And then you're aware, of course, that a book was published in 2001 called the Application of Rules of The International Law of Armed Conflicts, which is an exhibit in this case. I haven't got the number immediately. I can't read it. But you're aware of the publication of that book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that book published really as a piece of information for the ICTY to read, setting out, as it did, how well behaved the VJ was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the author and the publisher of that book had in mind except for presenting what was done by lower-level commands down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when General Pavkovic was being interviewed in great complexity, material was handed over that again included material going to show that the VJ was behaving properly. Were you involved in the preparation of the material that Pavkovic handed over or that was handed over on Pavkovic's behalf? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I'm suggesting to you, General Gojovic, that there has from the moment that this conflict started been an awareness of the need to make it look as though things were in place to conduct the war lawfully and to punish those who offended. That's my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the way it was acted, abiding by the provisions of international humanitarian law and also charges were brought by prosecutors where they had evidence against such perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm just going to round off my suggestion before we look at the next few documents. The extraordinarily limited number of convictions, the failure to convict anyone of a senior rank apart from possibly a major and a captain, the failure to investigate generals, the failure to investigate ethnic cleansing despite the widespread allegations being made, all show that this was a sham by the army, and you know it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not an omission on the part of the army, and you keep trying to convince me that this is something I know about and that it existed, but it did not exist. If any general had issued orders to commit a war crime, there would have been awareness of that, but there was no such general. You do not think that generals and commanders of brigades would order something like that. How could something like that cross your mind let alone how can you say it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again before we move on, we saw last week how, at the end of tab 18, there was an investigation into persons unknown for the bodies found at Izbica. You explained to us how it was that a passing unit had seen something and gone to investigate. Help us if you will, General: On your understanding, were the VJ units or whichever unit it was, were the VJ units first on the scene?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this information provided by the commander of the unit in question, it seems that when that unit came, it found freshly dug graves, many of them, and of course he found this to be suspicious, and he informed the prosecutor, who asked for measures to be taken in that respect, to carry out exhumations, and that was indeed done. Now, whether there was a unit there beforehand is something that I did not have any information about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I'd like you to consider, please, a document that is now available. It was not available when we were prosecuting -- when we were presenting the Kosovo part of the case. I think only in English, but there's a short passage to be read to you. It's only in English, I'm afraid, General, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't prepared the whole report. Of course it's available if people want it, but this is for value of only one purpose at this stage, in any event. And if the usher would place the front sheet on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is -- General, this is an activity report for 2002, 2004, by the Office of Missing Persons and Forensics of UNMIK. The second page, Mr. Nort, simply shows the table of contents. But on the third page I'm going to read something out to you, General. The report of UNMIK says this, middle paragraph: "Thus far, human remains recovered from mass graves in Serbia ... have been associated with known events of disappearance, each gravesite corresponding with a particular event: For example, bodies exhumed from Batajnica 2 site belong to those who went missing in Meja ... and those exhumed from Petrovo Selo belong to victims of the Izbica massacre." Now, at the moment this is the only material and evidence we have to make this point, but could you explain to us, please, how if the VJ was there and if your organisation was conducting a proper inquiry into and supervision of the mass gravesites at Izbica bodies were moved from there to Petrovo Selo in Serbia in order to hide them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask the people who did that, who were actually involved in the hiding. I cannot give you an answer to that. If this information is correct, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no way, is there, General, that a properly conducted forensic exercise into a mass crime, with the crime scene properly preserved, could permit of some of those bodies to be taken away and to be hidden in another territory.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exhumation was carried out, as far as the information I have is concerned, it was the end of May, beginning of June. It was reported on the 29th of May, so it was still the beginning of June when the aggression was still on, so appropriate action was taken. The prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was on your watch. And I want you to tell us, please, how on earth it could be that bodies taken in a proper forensic examination by investigating Judges and prosecutors could possibly have been taken away to be hidden. You tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please. After the burial and after all action that was taken and it was established what was found, 144 grave sites and 101 exhumations were carried out, and at that time that was the end of the job of the authorities involved. What happened subsequently is something that I cannot give you an answer about because I have no knowledge about that. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sat on this committee under the chairmanship of Terzic that dealt with requests for documents by the OTP to the VJ through the National Council for Cooperation. You tell us what documents exist that deal with the transportation of bodies from Kosovo to Batajnica, because it's not challenged that they did move from Kosovo to Batajnica and to Petrovo Selo. What documents exist?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents about their transfer, that is something that we never had. At the General Staff and in their archives, there is no such information. Ask those who concealed this. They probably know. Those who found them probably know how they got there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you must know. You moved -- you moved at the centre of VJ life for a long time. You tell us. Who moved those bodies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, throughout my testimony, you keep saying that it must have been somebody from the VJ. It was no one from the army of Yugoslavia. There is no such information. Had there been any such information, it would have been found. At least this commission and military prosecutors. Even if there were such transfers, it was done apart from the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on very quickly because I'm running out of time. You brought charges that led to about three or so convictions, half a dozen convictions and no more, but let's see what else you were prepared to devote your energies on. The document before you, I'm afraid -- it is in both languages, it is a document published by Natasa Kandic who runs a non-governmental organisation in Belgrade. The document was published on the 12th to the 13th of August of the year 2000. You can look at it very briefly and perhaps at more leisure if necessary and appropriate later, but she made serious allegations here about the conduct of the army, the FRY army, in the conflict, didn't she? Conflicts generally.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are all sorts of things in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us, please, what it was in the year 2000 that was so serious that you felt an obligation to have her charged with a criminal offence for writing criticism of the army when you couldn't and when your group couldn't investigate the ethnic cleansing itself. What was it in this article that was so grave that prompted you to try to prosecute Natasa Kandic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not prosecute Natasa Kandic. I did not. It is only the prosecutor who can prosecute her, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very rapidly at a sequence of events. The next document, we'll have a look at it, please, is the response of the army to this because it's right, isn't it, that there was a response?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. At that time, I was on annual leave when this happened, what Natasa talks about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say. All right. So just look at it. Mrs. Kandic Launches Grave But Groundless and Premature Accusations. To that she had the courage to reply on the 21st of August, and we can have a quick look at that and decide later whether we can apply to have them all produced, but just have a look at what was being said on the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming your way, Mr. Nort. This one we will just focus on for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So here is Natasa Kandic, executive director of the Humanitarian Law Centre, on the 21st of August. If it could go on the overhead projector, please. And amongst the things she refers to halfway down the page is the Yugoslavian army's response with secret trials. She alleges that she will not remain silent about the horrors of the generals who sent young recruits to witness things in Kosovo, and she said towards the foot of the page that she saw Albanian villages surrounded by tanks, she heard the shelling, she saw thousands of people leaving their homes and columns of civilians on the road. So this is a Serb, Serb woman in Belgrade who dares to challenge the army. Is that right, General Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Natasa Kandic and her arguments, I have a completely different opinion. First of all, Natasa Kandic does not have any institutions of a scientific nature behind her that would establish legally valid grounds. Her observations, aired through the media, she seems to see everything, hear everything. That is her own sense of observation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing there for a minute.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll look at the bottom of the page and tell you what she said publicly, realising that she faced the entire Yugoslav army. She said this, four lines up from the bottom of the page -- five: "I spoke with people who were in Izbica on the 26th of March." And she gives some accounts. Go over the page, please, Mr. Nort. Three lines down. Having dealt with somebody whose son was shot but not seen to be shot, she speaks of 10.000 civilians forced by shelling to leave a field. She goes on in the next paragraph, General Gojovic, to say to those whom she was addressing that these are the facts. "... this is the cruel truth about Izbica, Bela Crkva, Cuska, Vucitrn and many other places and not, as the army maintains 'falsehoods.'" And she says: "I stand here and plead guilty because I did nothing to prevent these crimes from being committed. You rebuke me for not praising the Yugoslav army ..." Let's go and see what that drew. That drew a further response from the army, saying it would sue Natasa Kandic. And then it drew this: This is a document, even if you were on leave, General Gojovic, that you're going to know about, because you signed it. While the document's coming your way, do you say Serbia and Montenegro is a place where there is freedom of speech? Do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is a decision that you signed on the 26th of September of the year 2000. And if Mr. Nort could put the English version on the overhead projector, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "A disciplinary investigation has been initiated against Djorovic Lakic, Lieutenant Colonel serving with the Federal Ministry of Defence ..." Next paragraph: " ... due to a reasonable suspicion that, in the capacity of a Lieutenant Colonel serving with the Legal Administration of the Federal Ministry of Defence, on 1 September 2000, when Colonel Mihajlovic, who was replacing the Chief of the Legal Administration of the Federal Ministry of Defence during his absence, in the capacity of a superior in the service, ordered him, based on the material submitted from the Yugoslav Army General Staff, to make draft criminal and offence charges against Natasa Kandic, Director of the Fund for Humanitarian Law from Belgrade, for corresponding criminal acts and a violation ensuing from her interview published in the paper 'Danas' for the 12th to the 13th of August, 2000, he failed to execute the issued order, as was his duty to do, instead he made an official record wherein, inter alia, he stated the following: 'Majority of her (Natasa's) views I deem fully justified and I fully share them with her, that is I share her opinion of those views...'" Pausing there, this was a man who was in Kosovo as part of your group and he identifies with the views of Natasa Kandic. Remind me again, is there freedom of speech in Serbia Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is not freedom of speech. This is presenting incorrect information without arguments by Natasa Kandic, and the General Staff says she should offer up arguments, not stories and rumours. And since you mentioned this lieutenant colonel, he received orders to make a draft, that is to see to the technical side, technical processing for a draft complaint to the prosecutor, a draft of that, and then the official would send it forward. Whether they would table it or not is another question, but it would go on for processing. So it wasn't up to Djorovic to assess whether there were grounds or no grounds. He was an official carrying out orders. Any orders not carried out in the service would be subject to liability and accountability and that is the foundation of every army in every state. So to bring that in this context is improper before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understand me, General Gojovic, why I ask these questions. First of all, just confirm that it is your signature on the page seeking to have this man prosecuted. It is your signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, it is, and I don't challenge that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The context is this: You and those working with you would do everything to shut up people like Natasa Kandic or Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic who were prepared to tell the truth or who were prepared to investigate people at the time, in order to defend the army, and that's exactly what you're doing here today.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djorovic had the possibility when he was a prosecutor to bring these charges and not when charges were taken out against him because of his conduct which were incompatible to the duties of an officer, let alone a prosecutor. So in this way he is trying to defend himself and then seeking assistance by linking himself with Natasa Kandic, just as if someone who was seriously ill would go to a soothsayer to seek help there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also, of course, had the courage to challenge you in another way. We'll look at the next document, please, which tells us more about you, I'm going to suggest. On the 7th of November of the year 2000, he made a complaint against you, Major General Gojovic. I don't have time to go through the document in detail, but just look at it. And this complaint was to the effect that you obliged everybody in your department to go and vote for this accused. He had the courage at that make that complaint against you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He brought in criminal complaints against many people, but they were all rejected. Why didn't he take this into his hands, the processing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally on the 13th of June of 2001, and it's a long document, we don't have time to go through it, but you'll be familiar with it and I've referred to it already this morning. I now bring it in in its chronological position. He made a complaint against unidentified judges of the military court about the fact that case files he was pursuing were not dealt with properly and matters of that sort. Do you remember this complaint?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but otherwise, it demonstrates his conduct and behaviour which ranks him among being assessed -- his capabilities being assessed for the army, and that is the way he behaves. He files reports against everybody. Yet when he is in a position of authority, he doesn't do so. Why didn't he name the judges? He knows them all. He is trying to mask the eyes of the public and brings up Natasa Kandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, he had no anxiety, did he, about naming you? He was brave enough to do that, and it needed bravery in your state, didn't it, to oppose the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why didn't he prosecute once the prosecutor rejected the criminal report? He has the power to do so and to take it into his own hands and be the prosecutor against me. He didn't dare to do that, whereas he had the possibility of doing so, so why didn't he? But when you go to court, you have to provide proof and evidence, so that's why he didn't dare to do so. And his writings speak about the rights that you say did not exist, both to file criminal reports and to make -- go public, but nobody prosecuted him. Of course, if he didn't carry out orders, then proceedings against him should be initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, so that I can focus your mind on the relevance of Djorovic's behaviour and conduct, a large number of the people running the military judicial system in Kosovo at the time of the conflict were reservists. Not very many with the experience that he had. And I'm going to suggest to you that it would have been extremely difficult for them and would have required great bravery on their part to try to force through the proper indicting of individuals if the authorities were against it, and that's one of the reasons tabs 17 and 18 are as slim as they are. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. That is not the correct assessment. It's quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on the question of who you were prepared to -- finally, on the question of who you were prepared or who the authorities were prepared to prosecute, do you remember the journalist Miroslav Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the man is. There was somebody in the press, but I didn't follow that. And when it comes to journalists, I'm not interested in that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a journalist who was prosecuted for saying things that were unappealing to the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were appealing or unappealing. That's up to the prosecutor, not the army. The prosecutor is not within the composition of the army, it's within the composition of the ministry, it comes under the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A small technical exercise next, please, and then I'm nearly done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got a visual aid. I don't necessarily suggest it becomes an exhibit, but I want to deal very briefly through this witness with the efforts of that have been made for us to get documentation so you will know the degree to which these documents are complete, and I'll ask him a couple of questions about provision of documents. I am afraid it hasn't yet been translated into B/C/S or Serbian but it's only a visual aid or aide-memoire or whatever you like for the time being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, you've already dealt with, as I've already suggested, requests for provision of documents and you will therefore confirm, I hope, that as long ago as May 2001 there was a request to provide all documents in connection with investigations or prosecutions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. before courts military or civilian. Do you remember that request?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that request, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November 2001 there was a request for documentation in respect of Racak. Do you remember that request?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That request wasn't directed towards us. It was returned to the competent authorities --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recollect that in July of 2002 there was a production of as little as eight files? In July 2002, there was the production of as little as eight files for cases - and when I say "files" each file may have only been a page or so - and then some records relating to Racak. Do you recollect the provision of those documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me answer. When you asked for the files of all criminal charges - I don't know if it was you or Madam Carla Del Ponte - technical assistance was sought because the courts technically were not able to -- did not have the technical resources to copy, photocopy, all those files for us to send you all the cases, and that is why technical assistance was sought to deal with that matter. That technical assistance did not arrive and it was for those reasons that those files were not given over to you. That is the sole reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the efforts continued with a request in August 2002 for documentation concerning sexual assaults committed by members of the VJ. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documentation was supplied for those cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in October 2002, there was another request for assistance in respect of court documents for the particular judgements of Mancic, Radivojevic, Tesic, and Seregi. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a judgement related to Mancic. That came later. And once again there were technical impossibilities. Technical assistance was sought but we weren't able to comply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Technical problems. Then on the 4th of November there was a meeting with Mrs. Tromp and Mr. Treanor. Amongst other things, you explained that tab 18, differently described, did exist and said if we wanted it we should apply for it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that but I didn't understand what subject or tab you're referring to. That's the part I didn't understand but I do remember the meeting where we did discuss it and there were -- technical assistance was brought up again. And technical assistance was promised but once again, for technical reasons, the courts were not able to photocopy the documents to complete the files and send them in, otherwise they would have been happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said November, I meant December. We move on then to 2003, taking it swiftly. On the 14th of April you were asked questions, really basically to the effect of is this all there is in respect of military court files, and the response to that came on the 11th of September with the document that is tab 18, that's item 1, and various other documents fully identified on this schedule but not very much material by way of further files. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of September, I wasn't in the commission. The commission was disbanded, and that's when problems occurred with respect to complying with the requests made by this Tribunal. The commission no longer worked as of the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, it was disbanded by, what, Minister Tadic, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the grounds that it was behaving badly, wrongly, improperly, and obstructing the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The main point was to prevent some evidence reaching President Milosevic for his Defence case and not to prevent the work of the OTP. Quite the contrary. The work of the OTP was promoted through the work of that commission. But what was endeavoured was to prevent evidence getting to the Defence, and that's why Minister Tadic was replaced, or disbanded it. There was no other reason. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to be quite clear about it, that the OTP has made every effort to get original files and all documentation, and the provision has been either what we have got in these papers today, a few other files, or the answer it can't be done for technical reasons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about original documents, you know that original documents are not given from any archive. All you can do is photocopy them and provide photocopies, not original documents, so with that respect --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we've made every effort to get copies of original files of prosecutions and all we've got is what's in these documents, tab 17 and 18, and a few other files that are listed in the document I've placed before the Judges. That's all we've been able to get from you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why didn't you provide technical assistance? You would have been provided with all the rest of the files you asked. So you didn't invest all efforts at your disposal. Technical efforts, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, was Tadic's official reason -- What was the official reason he gave for disbanding your commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give any official reasons. What came before was typical conduct; that is to say several articles appeared in the papers according to which some mysterious commission - which was verified, by the way - was preparing the Defence of Slobodan Milosevic. So it was on the basis of those newspaper articles that Tadic came to disband the commission without giving any reasons for doing so. So that was the first act that he signed as defence minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally this, then: You dealt with all requests from the time the commission was in existence. There is a body called the Joint Command, isn't there? Or wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want an answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I certainly --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came across the term from a document that came to the commission while it was still working. It was a document one and a half pages long and there was a heading there that said Joint Command. However, the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute. We can look at the documents but it takes time. Just confirm, please, that for the duration of the conflict in Kosovo between March and June of 1999, there was a body that ran things for Serbia and Montenegro and it was called the Joint Command, and it was called the Joint Command because it had representatives from civil authority, Sainovic, and the military.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I wasn't aware of that. I wasn't in that system of command. But I did come across that document later in the work of the commission and we were wondering about what the document was. It was the draft of an order without a signature, without a stamp. So that is the only thing I learnt about, that there might be some kind of body with that name, but what it was actually was I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the man in charge of the military judicial system. Please tell us, how was the conflict run and where can we find the records of how it was run, because all our efforts so far have been unsuccessful. How was the conflict run?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What conflict do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Response to NATO. How was it -- how was it managed? Who made the decisions? Who deployed the troops? Who made the decisions about the civilians? It was a Joint Command, wasn't it? You must know this, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please. You're mixing apples and pears here. All the orders went from the staff of the Supreme Command, and that was the system of command that was functioning. So if there was a body called the Joint Command that was just to dovetail and harmonise relations down there because there were organs of internal affairs, civilian protection there, and somebody had to coordinate all that, and their mutual actions, cooperation, working together, somebody had to do the job. But otherwise, the army functioned according to the principle of subordination from the Supreme Command to the lowest level unit. Now this auxiliary body, if it existed, it might have existed. That's nothing new. Quite obviously, civilian organs had to coordinate their affairs. You have to live down there, get supplies down there to the units, coordinate everything, so somebody had to be in charge of that and do the job. Whether the term was the right term and whether you're being misled by the term "Joint Command," that's another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't have time to do that, but just help me with this: We've had a lot of evidence in this case with VJ units being deployed, shepherding Kosovo Albanians out of their country, Macedonia, Albania. You've fielded, you've dealt with all the requests for detailed information and for documents from the OTP during the period you were on the commission. Where can we find the documents that will explain the deployment of those forces and explain what it is said they were doing? Because we want to know.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every action on the part of the army, every movement by the army would come after orders from a superior officer, and we have those orders. You don't wish to say, I assume, that orders -- by issuing orders you couldn't deploy the army to defend the country from attacks and giving artillery support and so on. That was the only case in the world in the history of warfare where this would have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no trouble, did you, providing 8.000 documents that concerned offences committed by the KLA, did you? No technical difficulty with doing that. Eight thousand pages.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done by the Ministry of the Interior. The Ministry of the Interior is quite a separate institution and organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very well. More efficient than yours? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly they're more efficient in cooperating and complying with your demands because they had the technical ability to do so and other support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't acknowledge the existence of something called a Joint Command, you know of something called the Supreme Defence Council that used to meet, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a constitutional institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the function of the Supreme Defence Council after the 26th of March of 1999, because we haven't been provided with any documents showing which body did, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from those documents, I didn't have an insight into the workings of the Supreme Defence Council. Their acts and orders and decisions didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, yes. I would ask for the sequence of documents that I presented to be exhibited. All of them bar the last one were acknowledge for what they were by the witness. The last one, the complaint by Djorovic in respect of his working as a prosecutor in May or thereabouts of 1999 was not acknowledged as a document by the witness but I don't think he denied the fact that such complaints were made by Djorovic, so I would ask that the Court to consider as admitting not only earlier documents but that last document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- our treatment of documents as an issue, and I for my part think it appropriate in the context in which you've now raised the matter to being cautious about -- particularly cautious about how we treat these, and I don't find it satisfactory just to be invited to exhibit these as a bunch of material without some sort of explanation of the evidential value that you see in each of these individually, because I think the responses of the general have varied among the documents. Now, can we take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm sorry to have attempted to deal with things more swiftly than was helpful but there's always the pressure of time. The first one, I think, is the publication of the 12th to 13th of August, 2000, and the Chamber will recognise that the burden of my questioning was to the effect that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me get the document. Which one was that, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the 12th to the 13th of August 2000 interview of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interview, yes. Okay. Now, what is the evidential value of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidential value of this document is that the reality of the general's approach, and indeed the reality of the approach of the authorities he represented, was that an article like this would draw an attempt to prosecute whereas there was no attempt to prosecute for the grave crimes being reported publicly, and that's the general burden of this sequence of exhibits. With that proposition in mind, the sequence of the reply by the army, which is the next one, that's the document that's titled "Mrs. Kandic Launches Grave But Groundless and Premature Accusations," the response by Mrs. Kandic of the 21st of August headed "HLC Executive Director's Letter to Yugoslav Army General Staff," which ends, in fact, on the same document with the response, "The army says it will sue Natasa Kandic" are all to the same theme, and they are the necessary preparatory material for consideration when the Chamber looks, if it would be good enough, to the document of the 26th of December signed by this witness where he initiates or signs in respect of a decision to initiate proceedings against Djorovic. So I would ask that those form a straightforward sequence and I would ask that they all be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come to -- but I'll stop there before I come to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand and I'm clear now about the purpose for which you seek these, simply to establish the fact that these things were written and the fact of the response thereto.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the next letter then the one that's headed "Military Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade"? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That still part of the same sequence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is -- no, the next one is a slightly different point. Military Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade is the complaint by Djorovic in respect of this witness that they were summoned in and required to vote for the accused, and this, of course, is a straight question of credit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well the problem with this is that I don't think you asked the witness the question, "Did you actually do this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore there's no evidential value if that's the purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, may I ask that question out of time? But that's the value of that one, and it's a credit issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would depend on there being evidence to support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may put the question Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Gojovic, you know this allegation made by Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic to the effect that on the morning of the 3rd of October of the year 2000 you summoned people to your office, instructing them as to how they should and when they should vote. You know about that allegation, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that allegation, but it was not correct. There was a meeting indeed but it had a completely different agenda. Current matters that was, yes, the second round of elections, and there was a lot of propaganda as to whether people would vote or not vote. So that has nothing to do with anything. It's not that I can issue orders to anyone on that score and it's not that anybody will vote in accordance with these orders. Voting is by secret ballot. The Constitutional Court had to rule on this, and indeed the court did prove that the first round of elections was not right, so then there had to be a run-off --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one other question -- sorry, Your Honour. You confirm that the elections were discussed in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not discussed. It wasn't an official meeting about elections. The official meeting was about something completely different, and then after that there were polemics among colleagues, but they are colleagues, co-workers. Whether people are going to vote or aren't going to vote, it was up to each and every individual himself. The official position of the court that was made public was that the first round of elections did not succeed in terms of the law, and that's the way it was. And why there was not a second round is something that you are fully aware of. So this was after the first round of voting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, were you aware that this complaint had been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first familiarised myself with this complaint when that group of lawyers manipulated it in their proceedings. So that is when I learned about it, after quite awhile. They referred to that complaint of his, and where it came from was something I had no idea about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't seek leave to ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I have one other document here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document is the one that I specifically set aside from the other series of documents when I made my comprehensive invitation to admit documents, and I set it aside because the witness did not acknowledge the existence of this complaint in this form. I think he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the one headed Criminal Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes. And this is a long document which deals with the Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic's view of events that happened in May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not asking for that to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I invited Your Honours to consider admitting it, but recognising that the witness hadn't acknowledged it as a complaint but had, I think, in the course of his testimony acknowledged that complaints of this kind were made by Djorovic, although he gave a different reason, if you'll remember, for Djorovic being sent back from Kosovo, saying it had to do with a fight and didn't have to do with these complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you ask to exhibit the summary of -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an aide-memoire for the Court. Of course it can be, if it's helpful, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about activity reports of MPF, of UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I ask for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The grounds for that are more difficult in the sense that they don't fall within any of our particularly recognised categories at the present. The position this, however: The witness comes to court and asserts that there is a legitimate or there has been, not a legitimate, a proper inquiry into the Izbica crime scene. It emerges, and it's emerged, of course, substantially since the close of the Kosovo evidence in this case, that there is material going to show that bodies from Izbica were hidden in Serbia. That would appear to be inconsistent with there being a properly conducted judicial investigation into the Izbica crime scene, and therefore I would ask that that material be admitted at this stage. There may, of course, be the opportunity to admit more evidence later, but to be admitted at this stage as some material going to counter the suggestion that this was a proper investigative process supervised to the extent that it was supervised by this witness. In this way, the argument's pretty much the same as the arguments we've been having over the recent weeks and months - not arguments, discussions - about the scope for admitting new material at the hand of the Prosecution in the course of the Defence case. We weren't to know until the witness came and gave evidence and gave his interpretation of document tab 18 what he would be saying, and it's in answer to that that this material will be of value to you. But it -- so it's consistent with earlier applications, perhaps slightly different. I think, incidentally, the position is, although I haven't yet found chapter and verse, that it has been indicated to the Chamber at an earlier stage that it might be necessary for us to seek to add evidence about exhumations in general and perhaps exhumations in Batajnica or Petrovo Selo in particular because the information was only coming available as the trial was progressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For that another time, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If Your Honours wanted to tell us first of all what was being ruled out and then that cuts things down, in my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think the two that are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Activity Report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the Criminal Report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the Criminal Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't disagree, then, with the findings of the Court, then, if the others are ruled in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We would like to hear about the Activity Report from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Activity Report, well, again, we've had evidence during the Prosecution case about the bodies being found in Serbia. That's already featured in evidence. This adds absolutely nothing. There's no reason for this to be made an exhibit at all. It has nothing to do with this witness. It's just another report from somewhere that comes into the case, it doesn't take any issue any further, and then is just left as an exhibit, almost hanging in the air, of no relevance to this witness when we've heard evidence already that in fact greatly amplifies in far greater detail in the Prosecution case the paragraph that we're looking at within this report. So in my submission, it simply doesn't take matters further. It's something that was described as ammunition for cross-examination, I remember Judge May saying at one stage of the proceedings. Ammunition for cross-examination and no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The other side of the coin would be that there would be no harm in admitting this one. Therefore, there's already evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is harm because there is the amount of material we have to deal with. We don't know whether we have to file a response to it in a closing brief, how we have to deal with it, and it multiplies the material unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to me there's a point of principle involved here, because while this particular one might be harmless - may be, I say no more than that - if the principle is that the Prosecution can present freestanding material in the course of cross-examination, then we could come against, at a later stage, some very significant piece of material that we would have exactly the same point to decide about, and that's what concerns me. While this particular one may be of no great significance, I'm more concerned about the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. That's our position on it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. That's our position on it. These things build up. You then have to find them. You have to -- and they're not actually hung onto anything within the proceedings themselves but they're lying there, perhaps as a dormant bomb that could have some significance that hasn't been dealt with at the time. In relation to the criminal report, he didn't know anything about it, and in our submission it doesn't take anything any further. It doesn't come into these proceedings in any way. It has no real relevance to the issues that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Milosevic, just on these two, the two documents, the Activity Report and the Criminal Report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand that you were talking about the UNMIK Activity Report. You were talking about the Activity Report of the MPF, weren't you, or perhaps I misunderstood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's the Activity Report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may comment on the other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. May I start now or are you taking the break now? I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear you on this and then we'll take a break. I don't imagine you'll be very long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. You don't have anything to say on the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In relation to this, I just asked you whether you were talking about the MPF document or the UNMIK document. That's what I asked you. That's the clarification I sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I reply in two sentences? With Your Honours' leave, may I reply in two sentences? As to the UNMIK document so described, it is, I think, new material because thus far I don't think there was a connection between Izbica and the burial sites in Serbia. There's a connection between Meja and Batajnica and so on, so it's new on that. On the other point, it is material that is significant because of course if it be the case that somebody was thwarted from doing his conscientious task as a military prosecutor, then that would be important in relation to this witness's evidence. So it is potentially significant. That doesn't determine the question of its admission, but I don't accept that it's not potentially important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In relation to this material that, as Mr. Nice just said, linked up some graves in Serbia to the victims, the dead from Izbica, Mr. Bonomy commented and said that this is not harmful to the Defence or, rather, that it did not harm the Defence in any way. I would like to add something to that. It's helpful to the Defence, as a matter of fact, because I wish to draw your attention to the following: This witness, in the documents that you saw, he provided documents and testified that on the 29th of May, our organs - that was 1999 - discovered corpses in Izbica. As a matter of fact, an exhumation was carried out of 101 corpses and also a forensic analysis and so on. And now indeed a question is raised in the minds of all who are listening to this, watching this, and particularly in your minds, gentlemen, when there is a case dating back to the 25th of May, when an exhumation was carried out, a forensic analysis, et cetera, what would be in somebody's interest, to take these bodies somewhere to Serbia and to hide them? These bodies have to do with criminal proceedings that started during the war, as far back as that. That is something that is incomprehensible to any person who is sensible and reasonable. Then we will finally get to the background involved, how and where and when these bodies were buried in Serbia. But this link indubitably shows that there was an active criminal case as from May 1999. The bodies had even been exhumed then. Why and who did this? That would have to be established in order to explain things. So I'm not opposing admitting this into evidence at all. As for the Criminal Report, I don't know what you exactly mean, because Mr. Nice kept using the same expressions. He said in a very meaningful manner what Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic thought of what was being done. I think that this needs to be admitted in order to show that Mr. Nice is mystifying things. Lieutenant Colonel Djorovic, in this Criminal Report, does not raise the question of concealing any document whatsoever in relation to the crimes that are being prosecuted, in terms of war crimes, violations of humanitarian law, et cetera. This entire Criminal Report of several pages has to do with thefts only, 17 cases, and it's obvious that all of them were returned by the end of May. This was some kind of manipulation, if that's the right word. It all boils down to robbery, theft. Mr. Nice held it against General Gojovic that in statistics there are many crimes of theft, robbery, et cetera. Well, they're there because they are crimes, and as a rule they are the most numerous ones. If you read this Criminal Report, I don't think you've read it in the meantime, but read it and you will see that each and every letter in this document has to do with the make of a particular car, chassis number, and so on and so forth. It has to do with cassette players, TV sets, and so on and so forth. Robbery, theft only, not hiding documents that would indicate theft of -- I mean, not concealing documents that would have to do with any serious violations of humanitarian law or killings, rapes, attempted murders, and so on. So this Criminal Report is something that you can look at and you will see that he did not even refer to any documents that had to do with violations of humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you actually see this document as being of assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is useless, worthless. I commented upon this because Mr. Nice was mystifying matters. He was saying that somebody was concealing something and then this honest lieutenant colonel comes in and indicates that there was a lack of prosecution of such crimes. And that is simply incorrect. It only has to do with theft. Of course that is a crime, too, but that is far away from all the things that we are discussing here. Whether somebody stole a vehicle is something that local courts of law should deal with. It has nothing to do with the matters at hand here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. At the end of the break, we'll give our ruling which will demystify matters. We will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit all of the documents put forward by the Prosecutor. In doing so, we would in particular note the agreement of the accused with the admission of the last two, the Activity Report and the Criminal Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm much obliged and I also apologise for having attempted to take things too swiftly. It's one of the problems with living under the pressure of watching the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you get through it, Mr. Nice, so much the better. The numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 840 will be for the Activity Report 2000 20004. The interview with Danas will be 841. The next, Kandic Lunches Grave But Groundless and Premature Allegations will be 842. 843 for the document dated 21st of August, 2000. 844 for the decision dated 26th of September, 2000. 845 for the Military Prosecutor's Office dated 7th of November, 2000. 846, the Criminal Report. And 847 for the summary of Prosecution requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Gojovic, Mr. Nice this morning at the beginning of our session asked you a number of questions with respect to the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Sarajevo. I am bearing in mind the fact that last week, when speaking of the matter, said the court was in the Viktor Bubanj barracks, the investigating prison, the detention centre, military -- police -- military police company and some other organisations. So they were all housed on the premises of the barracks. And it was noted that 120 people was how much the military police company numbered which provided security for the prison and the court. From the military aspect, could the Viktor Bubanj Barracks be considered a location of a combat unit in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an institution. It was where the unit was accommodated and that's why the place was called the Viktor Bubanj Barracks, but otherwise they were all military institutions that were housed there. The court, the prosecutor's office, the land surveyance office, and that part was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We cleared that matter up. Mr. Nice said that if an effective prosecutors and military system existed, which means he claims one didn't exist, and I took a note of this, he also said that there was no attempt made to prosecute serious crimes. I made a note of him saying that. Now, in that connection, I would like to refer you back first of all to tab 14. And tab 14, on page 1, provides a list of convictions and on page 2 a list of accused. Now, General Gojovic, I'm not going to look at the other columns, just crimes against life and limb, that particular column, and in the second list, and we'll go back to list one, 55 individuals were accused of crimes against life and limb. Is that what it says here, the total figure in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that the date there is as of the 15th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, 55 persons were accused of these crimes as of the 15th of May, 1992, for crimes against life and limb alone, which means that in the first 50 days -- that was within the first 50 days of the NATO aggression; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that in Kosovo, there was bombing round the clock, 24 hours every day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. Not only Kosovo but throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but especially in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially in Kosovo. That was the photo point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that 16.000 tonnes of bombs fell on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were facts and figures to that effect. There were enormous quantities. I'm not sure of the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last week you said that the units and institutions and courts and the prosecutors' offices would relocate, move their locations to avoid the bombing very frequently; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So under those conditions nonetheless of round the clock bombing during the war just up until the 15th of May, 55 persons were accused of crimes against life and limb, and as we can see in the first table, 6 plus 2 gives us 8, 8 were convicted per category of person and type of crime for crimes against life and limb. Six plus 2 persons convicted.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. General, do you have any information as to the circumstances in which these crimes would have been committed? It's fairly general here, "crimes against life and limb." What types of crimes are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are crimes against life and limb, as it says; wherever human life came into question, killings, et cetera. And these were mostly killings. And tab 18 gives you a review up until the 20th of June, 1999. 188 were convicted and 382 court proceedings were taken for this particular category of crime against life and limb against the civilian population, multiple killings, attempts at killings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, in view of the circumstances that the military judiciary organs, law enforcement organs, the police function, the commands and other institutions during the bombing, do you as a professional judge, prosecutor, and chief the legal department in the General Staff think and assess that this is a high degree of efficiency or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, no, Mr. Milosevic. It's very tendentious and leading. "Do you think it's a high degree?" He will say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No, I hadn't completed my question. What I wanted to ask him is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a high level of efficiency, average, or low level of efficiency? How would you in view of your professional experience categorise this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we bear in mind the fact that 2.811 persons were convicted in two months, the first verdict came in around the 1st of April, 1991, and over 6.000 were accused, 6.000 accused, and in the first instance 2.811 convictions were passed means a high degree, without doubt. Now, in that figure, we could not have included all the serious crimes which required complex investigation and proof, but if you look at the figure itself, it speaks for itself, self-evident. And no court even in peacetime can achieve such a high level of efficiency in practice. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I have been following the practice and efficiency of courts for a very long time now, since 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, could you just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, just clarify: These are all crimes committed by soldiers, military offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crimes I'm talking about, yes, just members of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we were saying, in no respect were these crimes, the crimes that the military judiciary worked on, incorporated crimes which the civilian judiciary had under their jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now take a look at tab 18, please. It is page 4 in the English version and 2 in the B/C/S. So B/C/S 2 is English 4. And there you have war crimes against the civilian population, against civilians. I'm just going to dwell on that for a short time because Mr. Nice last week asked a question relating to that from which it emerged that it was soldiers that were taken out of prison and then engaged in shooting, and he said he would go back to that but he didn't in fact to it, so I have to do that now. What it says here is this -- I haven't got the English translation but I suppose it's the same in English. The accused's names are given, and then it says: "With premeditation killed 5 unidentified Albanians whom they had previously taken prisoner and detained during an operation by their unit. Having taken them out of custody, they put them against the wall of a house, opened fire on them with automatic rifles, and killed them all. They threw them into a well into which they poured petrol and then set it on fire." Now, is it clear from that that these individuals or, rather, the individuals who were killed were taken out of detention? It wasn't the soldiers that were taken out of detention and committed a crime, it was these individuals who were taken out of detention.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, from page 2 onwards and up to page 19, where serious instances of theft, looting -- on page 17 armed robbery, for example, including killing, that is why they are grievous crimes because armed robbery with killing took place. So over those 17 pages we have the names and surnames of the perpetrators who were known to have committed the crime, and they include 25 individuals.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is shown at the beginning, the summary review. The total number is given there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you count them, all the names and surnames, this gives us 25 in total. Now, in the column to initiate proceedings, which means once the information has been collected and ruling to initiate proceedings goes through, can we see when the proceedings were initiated? It is page 4 of the English version. It gives us the date, the 4th of August, then the 10th of June, all in 1999. The 2nd -- the 22nd of May is the next date. Then we have the 4th of June, 1999, and the 21st of May, 17th of May, 15th of June, 25th of April, and May 1999. Then once again we take it from the 26th of May, the 11th of May, the 4th of May, the 9th of May, and so on and so forth, ruling to initiate proceedings on those dates. All the most serious crimes were initiated during the situation of war, state of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it. And I said that this column entitled ruling to initiate proceedings is a ruling brought by the investigating judge. The military prosecutor before that already had information, gathered the information, checked it out and then sent in a request for an investigation to be launched to the court. Once a court order was made to initiate proceedings, then according to our law, we have the ruling to initiate proceedings. That's when the proceedings were initiated. Everything is the pre-trial stage, done by the investigating organs. So the prosecutor learnt about this far earlier than the dates recorded here, but these are the first dates recorded so that we know exactly when proceedings were initiated. And all these cases came to trial on these dates during the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let's just clear one more thing up. A moment ago in giving your explanations to a question asked you by Mr. Nice, you said something about crimes here, and you said that some of the crimes were processed or, rather, they were qualified to begin with as killing -- multiple killings, and then the indictment was changed to a charge of war crimes. Could you clear one matter up, please: Did the prosecutors, when qualifying the crime and bringing in an indictment, did they opt for a more serious qualification or a less serious one?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that. Wherever there was not sufficient information, proof, and evidence, where there was an order from a superior officer that killings should be perpetrated, always sought the more serious qualification of killings of two or more people, multiple killings. And according to republican law, this provided for the death sentence, and the lowest sentence was ten years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So I just wanted to clear that point up. Now, let me summarise: If he starts off with a more serious qualification, then the prosecutor can commute this to an easier, to a lighter sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he starts off with a lighter qualification, can he commute it to a more serious one, a graver one?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cannot do this during the proceedings, requalify it and change the charge, so that's the way they worked to give them more manoeuvering space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to our laws, multiple killing, is that a more serious qualification, because it invokes the death sentence, than a war crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far more serious. Not only does it invoke the death sentence but the minimum prison term is 10 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean for multiple killings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So something starts out with multiple killing and then ends with this lighter qualification of war crime, is that it? Is that the process and that's what you tried to explain to us in your response to Mr. Nice's question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, in view of the fact that we are discussing the question of whether all these crimes were prosecuted, whether they were uncovered, the perpetrators brought to justice, et cetera, you've already explained that to us. But may we -- would you give me a specific answer to my question now. Was there a single case of a crime having been committed for which the organs of Yugoslavia -- when I say "organs of Yugoslavia" I mean from the topmost to the lowest organs of the judiciary, the law enforcement organs or whichever other organs in that context -- was there a single case of a crime for which the organs knew about but didn't prosecute?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of a case like that. All the crimes that were known to have been committed were prosecuted by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
