utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Nice dwelt in particular on one point and I'd like to ask you to give us an explanation. He dwelt on tab 17 for some time, page 43, in fact, in the B/C/S, in the Serbian version, and I think he said that it was page 56 in the English version. And under number 7 --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 43 in Serbian, 56 in English of tab 17. Yes, that's right. And he pointed that page out to you and drew your attention to the fact that it was page 56 in the English version. Now, under number 7 we have here proceedings against a lieutenant colonel and four soldiers, privates. And then he asked you to explain or clarify -- or, rather, he suggested that it was the lower ranks that were prosecuted but not the higher ranks. Now, looking at this example that the proceedings were interrupted with respect to the lieutenant colonel, these legal proceedings with respect to the lieutenant colonel, were they stopped because he was a lieutenant colonel or was there any legal reasons for the proceedings to be interrupted with respect to that individual?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't because he was a lieutenant colonel. Quite the contrary. As far as I can see from this, he was a security officer and as these were individuals who were detained, he investigated the reasons for that, and then the soldiers who are listed here took these people out of detention without his knowledge and permission and put them up against a wall and shot them. So that is why proceedings were brought against the lieutenant colonel and these individuals, but it was established that they did this on their -- of their own accord without instructions or orders from the lieutenant colonel. That is why the case was stopped. There was no reason to prosecute the lieutenant colonel. And these privates went on to commit other cases. This came group of men, under B, were responsible for the second crime, too. So that makes a total of seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that the proceedings -- the lieutenant colonel was prosecuted to begin with because he was the senior officer, but the legal proceedings were stopped because it was established that he never knew that they had -- they were not following his orders, and they did not take these people out of detention, shoot them, following his orders, that he had no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw a clip that was played here by Mr. Nice. Many civilians could be seen. I don't know whether you noticed that the recording starts with a commentary and an image. It is the border of Yugoslavia. You can see the Yugoslav flag there, and I assume that the Serbian flag is there, too, but they went over that very quickly. And then the reporter says, "Under the symbols of Serbian nationalism, the authorities are expelling the Albanians." A state flag that is at a border crossing, can that be considered a symbol of Serbian nationalism under which Albanians are being expelled?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only natural that everybody knows that, but this reporter sounded like a sports commentator covering a football game. He really got carried away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it quite clear that this is propaganda, that this is propaganda information that is given tendentiously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing that, Mr. Milosevic. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on, he says, "The Serb forces are moving from the outskirts of Kosovo towards Pristina," as if the army of Yugoslavia is taking Kosovo, conquering Kosovo. Do you know that the units of the army of Yugoslavia then and before that and for years before that were in Pristina itself, which is to say that it is not some kind of a movement from the outskirts towards Pristina; this is an integral territory where the army was. The army was throughout the territory. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Kosovo and Metohija, there were several military garrisons where there were military units, even in peacetime let alone in wartime. So that statement in itself by the reporter disqualifies his own conduct, as if Kosovo were a separate state entity of another state and that these military forces were now invading it. So he is saying something that is quite contrary to the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice suggests that what was planned was some kind of ethnic cleansing. General, do you know -- or, rather, he mentioned reports in the world public about the expulsion of Albanians. Do you know, General, that this story about ethnic cleansing was invented in order to justify an illegal aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you continue like that, I'll terminate the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave explanations about the establishment of war courts in accordance with the law. General, military courts have existed throughout; for as long as there's been a state; for many years.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred sixty years without any interruption. That anniversary was commemorated last year, of the military judiciary, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Isn't it quite clear in the law that if a state of law is declared, by virtue of that fact military courts are turned into war courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an imperative legal provision that war courts are established in a state of war once a state of war is declared. The war military establishment is developed in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This wartime military establishment, how much bigger was it than the peacetime establishment? What were the numbers involved when you compare the two?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to wartime establishment, there were 20 first instance courts and four second instance courts whereas in peacetime there were only three courts, one -- two first instance courts and a third court of appeals, a second instance court. And hence there are appropriate prosecution offices with a total of over 60 people, and this way there were 155 judges and -- judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not going into all the persons mentioned in tabs 17 and 18, Mr. Nice asked you about one or two cases. I'm not sure about that. I think it was two cases. Who started the proceedings, whose initiative it was and so on. In response to the question put by me as to whether these documents were accessible to the public, you said yes last week; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that all the relevant facts are included there in all these individual cases, and can it be established who started the proceedings and how this was dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This exists in every case file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for all the persons mentioned here, are there case files with the judiciary institutions in charge in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all dealt with by military courts, especially the military court in Nis, and now they were handed over to the district court in Nis because towards the end of last year, military courts ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice put a question to you that had to do with cooperation with UNMIK. Before I ask you about this cooperation in greater detail, I have a few preliminary questions. General, do you know how many Serbs, Montenegrins, and non-Albanians in general were expelled from Kosovo and Metohija from the moment when the UN took over in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically the entire population. A very small number remained. I cannot give you the exact number, but most of these people were expelled before the very eyes of the representatives of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many Serbs and non-Albanians, including even some Albanians, were killed under the authority of UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many who were killed and kidnapped; over a thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many monasteries and churches were destroyed during UNMIK authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is a very high one, going up to 180. I don't know the exact figure, but this has to do with major historic landmarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many tens of thousands of homes and properties of Serb families were destroyed under UNMIK authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great many. Over 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what the witness is answering to and what the question really means, speaking about UNMIK and saying under their authority. I'm not sure that the matter really arises for re-examination but if he wants to ask it, he can, but at least we ought to know if it's being said that UNMIK in some way authorised these things. I'm not sure what's being suggested and what the witness thinks he's answering to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not -- it's not very clear that this does arise out of cross-examination, but in any event, we need to have this clarified, the question "Do you know how many monasteries and churches were destroyed during UNMIK authority," which would appear to suggest that the destruction of the monasteries occurred somehow with the connivance or the support of UNMIK. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, there is no doubt that with 10.000 policemen we kept law and order in Kosovo, and the UN cannot prevent this many crimes with 40.000 soldiers. One cannot talk about any kind of active role on their part in protecting the population. Under the contrary: Under their auspices, the greatest crimes happened. 300.000 persons were expelled. Churches and monasteries were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you would have no evidence, would you, to say that UNMIK supported or promoted the destruction of these monasteries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there are even videotapes that show soldiers of the forces in Kosovo now just standing there while the churches and monasteries are in flames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing any more questions on these preliminary matters. Move to the main subject area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same UNMIK that you addressed and that you said did not give any response to requests made by the military judiciary organs in order to get legal assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the prosecutor and the court addressed the judiciary organs in Kosovo under UNMIK auspices in order to get assistance and that their requests were not met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I mentioned all the crimes that were committed, and that's a well known fact. Do you know how many perpetrators in Kosovo were convicted of the crimes that I mentioned to you just now, or at least arrested on account of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such information, how many people were arrested, how many people were convicted. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the authorities of Serbia or, rather, the organs of Serbia sought cooperation in terms of crimes committed by very precisely defined individuals, like Agim Ceku, Hashim Thaci and others? Was there any cooperation there with UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that Ceku was arrested at an airport in Hungary, I believe, speaks in itself, but he was released due to UNMIK intervention, although there are proceedings instituted against him in a court of law in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of assistance did you seek from UNMIK, the one that was not given to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with a few crimes, including rape, and it also has to do with the victim in that case, that she be brought to the court of law where her safety would be guaranteed. However, this was not done. She Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. needed to be heard by the court directly. However, that did not happen. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, Izbica was mentioned here. Tell us what you know about Izbica. What was done in relation to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am not allowing you to re-examine that. Izbica was mentioned. If you have a specific question arising out of something that was asked in cross-examination about Izbica, then you may re-examine on it, but not just, "Tell us what you know about Izbica." If you don't have a specific question relating to something that arose in cross-examination about Izbica, then move on to another matter. You are spending too much time in re-examination, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Mr. Nice linked the bodies from Izbica to the graves in Serbia. I hope that it's clear in whose interest this could have been, whether this could have been the interest of the state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've cut you off. You are evidencing a reckless disregard for the rules, and if you continue like this, we will terminate the re-examination and you call your next witness. You're moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what was the number of corpses that our authorities found in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred forty-four freshly dug graves. 101 bodies were exhumed. There are files about all of this. One hundred forty-four graves were found. How this happened, how come these corpses happened to be in the grave in Batajnica is a different question altogether, and it requires new explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read the Kosovo indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the number referred to there as far as Izbica's concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few numbers are mentioned there, but the final figure is 118 plus 2, so 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that our authorities established as far back as May 1999 the proceedings started on the 29th of May, 1999, that they uncovered even more bodies?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'm not going to ask you about Izbica any longer. Mr. Nice, in his cross-examination - this does not have to do with you personally although he was dealing with you personally - he put a question to you in relation to your master's degree, that in order to be promoted to the rank of general, a master's degree is required. What are the regulations in Yugoslavia in order to have somebody appointed to the rank of general? It can only be a colonel who can become a general. Does such a person have to have a master 's degree?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be promoted to the rank of general, as far as the legal services are concerned, a doctorate is required. That is in peacetime. However, during a state of war, other regulations are applied, and there is a particular article in the law of the army of Yugoslavia that spells this out. In that case it is necessary to man all the required units and therefore a person has to manifest successful command and war merits. That is the requirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is as far as legal services are concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about generals who are not in the legal services? For regular generals, do you need to have a master's degree?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They need to have different kind of military schools completed, not like the ones in civilian life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to say don't worry about that. Nothing turns on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to spend a minute on this text that you got. This is the text that Mr. Nice said he did not have in Serbian but only in English. "[In English] Summary of Prosecution requests for assistance concerning records of investigations and prosecutions of members of the VJ..." [Interpretation] I'm just going to read one part where you are mentioned by name. This was the meeting held on the 4th of December, 2002, and then it says -- [Previous translation continues] I think that refers to the army centre, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it says "Meeting at 'VJ house,'" the VJ house is in fact the army centre; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one was in the army centre and one was in the Ministry for External Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, but this was at the VJ house or army centre, and this is what it says -- among other things, you were present, and you say, or, rather, it says: "[In English] General Gojovic reported that many of the recent military cases from Kosovo were still in progress and others were transferred to civilian courts. Of 382 such cases, 188 resulted in conviction in military courts and an additional 137 had been transferred. There were also a number of cases involving the deaths of 580 persons where the perpetrators were still under investigation by military or civilian authorities..." [Interpretation] And so on. Now, was that the overall statistics that you had available at that point in time about the cases in which the organs of the -- of Yugoslavia were involved?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are facts and figures in tab 18, the summary review, with 382 cases, 188 resulted in convictions, and 137 were transferred to the competent civilian courts. The only other figure, this 580, it was actually 598 persons. That should be the correct figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the result of this summary review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I see. Thank you, General Gojovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General Gojovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Judge Danica Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may commence. Bear in mind we only have about seven minutes. There is another trial here this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Marinkovic, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1951 in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Macedonian by ethnicity. My maiden name was Drakulovska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what education do you have? Which schools, where and when?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed gymnasium or secondary school in the faculty of law in Skopje, Macedonia, in the Macedonian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us briefly when you graduated from university.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of law in 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I began work as a trainee in the law in the municipal court in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work after that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After one year, I took my bar examination before a committee of the Ministry of Justice in Macedonia, in Skopje, and having passed the examination, I went to live with my family in Pristina where I began working as an expert associate in the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you elected judge of the municipal court in -- or district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was elected judge of the district court in Pristina in 1984.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you start working as an investigating judge of the district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I began working as an investigating judge in November 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, you said you were elected as judge? Elected by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the Municipal Assembly of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, interpreter's correction: The Provincial Assembly of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]: Mr. Kwon, the National Assembly appoints judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it an appointment or election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's called the election of Judges whereas -- might I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let Mrs. Marinkovic explain. She knows more about that than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sure she does.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges are elected, so once a judge is elected by the Assembly, after they take the oath of office in front of the Assembly electing him, he begins working or she begins working as judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, would you explain to us in the briefest possible terms how the Assembly elects judges. How were you yourself elected a judge? Did you -- was there a public competition and you put your name down, or what are the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I shall explain. The election of -- there is a public competition that appears in the information media prescribing the conditions according to the law that each candidate must comply with in order to take part, the requirements. And once you put your name down, the candidates are checked out to see that they have the necessary requirements, and then the proceedings are sent on to the Assembly. There is a commission set up to review all the documents submitted for each candidate, and then it makes its decision as to the candidates and puts their names forward to the Assembly and then the Assembly elects -- makes the final election.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to compete, what requirements must you have?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: For a candidate to put his name down and apply for a judge, they must have graduated from the faculty of law, they must have passed the bar examination, and must have a certain amount of years of service depending on the court he is applying to, whether the district court or the municipal court. For the municipal court, three years of service were required, and for a district court judge, at least seven years of experience were required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. In paragraph 87 of the Kosovo indictment, and I'm going to quote that paragraph to you now: "After in --" "After Kosovo's autonomy was effectively revoked in 1989, the political situation in Kosovo became more and more divisive. Throughout late 1990 and 1991 thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police and civil servants were dismissed from their positions. The local court in Kosovo was abolished and many judges removed. Police violence against Kosovo Albanians increased." First of all, Mrs. Marinkovic, I've read out that paragraph, paragraph 87 from the indictment. Is what is alleged here true?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: From what you have just read out is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, since we have heard the statements by various witnesses pertaining to the general situation that is being described here, and in view of the individual professions mentioned, I am going to ask you questions and in doing so I shall be guided by the fact that you yourself are a judge. So I'm going to ask you about judges. It says many judges, so as a judge with many years of experience in the judiciary in Kosovo and Metohija, as a judge yourself, in other words, would -- may we have your comments on this paragraph, bearing in mind the situation in the judicial organs. Or, let me be more precise and concrete: How many judges were dismissed in 1990? And I'm bearing in mind what you know. The district court in Pristina, which is where you worked at the time, you told us that a moment ago, and the municipal court in Pristina, I assume you know about the situation in those two courts of law.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before I answer your question, might I be allowed to say or, rather, to give some explanations, with the Trial Chamber's indulgence? The local courts mentioned in the indictment, the local court in Kosovo was abolished, it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will hear the explanations and the answer tomorrow because we now have to adjourn. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.
